title: NSS Feed Output Format: Email DLP Logs

blocks.text: The Email Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Nanolog Streaming Service (NSS) feed specifies the data from the Email DLP logs that the NSS sends to the security information and event management (SIEM) system. You can configure an NSS feed by including one or more fields. The fields and their values display in the NSS feed output.

blocks.text: The following tables display information about the Email DLP log fields and possible values for those fields.
The following are date and time fields:

table: The log time (i.e., when a transaction is logged by the Zscaler Nanolog)
The feed time (i.e., when a transaction is received by the NSS from the Nanolog)
Seconds (0–59) as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
Minutes (0–59) as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
Hours (0–23) as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
The day of the week as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
The day of the month (1–31) as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
The name of the month as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
The month of the year as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
Year as recorded in the feed time (%s{rtime})
The time zone. This is the same as the time zone you specified when you configured the NSS feed.

blocks.text: The following are data center information fields:

table: The name of the data center
The city where the data center is located
The country where the data center is located

blocks.text: The following are user information fields:

table: The user who sent the email and is provisioned to Internet Access (ZIA)

The user who sent the email but is not provisioned to Internet Access. The external user can be within your organization. For example, a new employee joins the company and their company email address is created but their user account is not configured in the Zscaler Admin Console. In this case, the employee is treated as an external or "non-provisioned" user even though they are part of the company and can send email from their official company email address.

The username or email address of the user who sent the email. This field is an aggregate of %s{username} and %s{extusername}. If the user is provisioned to Internet Access, they populate in %s{username} and %s{owner}. If the user is not provisioned to Internet Access, they populate in %s{extusername} and %s{owner}. The fields %s{username} and %s{extusername} are not populated at the same time. The field %s{owner} is always populated whether the user is provisioned to Internet Access or not.

The username or email address of the user who sent the email. This field is an aggregate of %s{username} and %s{extusername}. If the user is provisioned to Internet Access, they populate in %s{username} and %s{sender}. If the user is not provisioned to Internet Access, they populate in %s{extusername} and %s{sender}. The fields %s{username} and %s{extusername} are not populated at the same time. The field %s{sender} is always populated whether the user is provisioned to Internet Access or not.

blocks.text: The following are email information fields:

table: The date and time at which the user sent the email
The date and time at which Zscaler received the email
The date and time at which Zscaler sent the email
The date and time at which the email was sent in epoch format
The name of the email tenant
The name of the email application
The MD5 hash of the email attachment
The size of the email attachment in bytes
The file type of the email attachment
The document type of the email attachment
The document subtype of the email attachment
[Banking Documents: Deposit or Withdraw Slips|Performance Management Documents: Performance Improvement Plans (PIPs)]
The file name of the email attachment
The recipients of an email that triggered a DLP rule (i.e., an action was taken)
The recipients of an email that did not trigger a DLP rule (i.e., no action was taken)
The domain of the recipients of an email that triggered a DLP rule (i.e., an action was taken)
The domain of the recipients of an email that did not trigger a DLP rule (i.e., no action was taken)
The DLP engine scan time, i.e., the duration of time from when Zscaler receives an email until policy evaluation is complete in milliseconds
The name of the DLP dictionary
The number of hits for each of the DLP dictionaries
The name of the DLP engine

The type of record (i.e., DLP Incident, Sensitive Activity, or Scan). A DLP incident means that a DLP rule violation was detected. A sensitive activity means that movement of sensitive data was detected. A scan is considered normal (i.e., no DLP rule violation or movement of sensitive data was detected).

The severity. A DLP incident violates a DLP rule and the severity (i.e., High, Medium, Low, Information) is based on the rule that was violated. A sensitive activity does not violate a rule but is reported for visibility (i.e., Information). A scan does not violate a rule and the field displays NA.

The action taken (i.e., Allow, Block, Custom Header Insertion). The Zscaler service either allows or blocks transactions. Other actions (e.g., quarantine) are taken by the email application (e.g., Microsoft Exchange) as defined by a custom header (e.g., X-Zscaler-Scan:Quarantine).
The name of the DLP rule

blocks.text: A SIEM can have parsing issues whenever a string field has non-printable or delimiter characters. For that reason, the Zscaler service has URL encoding for URL fields like URL, Referrer, and Hostname. There are several other fields that have the same parsing issue, but URL encoding is not suitable. Such fields are encoded using Base64.
Turning on Base64 encoding for all supported fields might result in approximately a 20% drop in performance.

The Zscaler service hex encodes all non-printable ASCII characters that are in URLs when it sends logs to the NSS. Any URL character that is less than or equal to 0x20, or greater than or equal to 0x7F, is encoded as %HH. This ensures that your SIEM can parse the URLs that contain control characters. For example, a \n character in a URL is encoded as %0A, and a space is encoded as %20.
